# Assignment 3: Naive Bayes Classification

## Objective

In this assignment, I am using the UniversalBank.csv dataset to see how credit card usage and online banking behaviour influence whether a customer accepts a personal loan or not. I'll be using pivot tables and Naive Bayes modeling to find the probability of a loan acceptance.


## Data Preparation

Out of the 5,000 customer records in the UniversalBank dataset, I used 60% (3,000 records) as the training set and kept the remaining 40% (2,000 records) for validation.

```{r data-preparation}
bank <- read.csv("C:/Users/Mahathi Kalluri/Downloads/UniversalBank.csv")

set.seed(123)
train_rows <- sample(1:nrow(bank), 3000)
train <- bank[train_rows, ]
validation <- bank[-train_rows, ]

dim(train)
dim(validation)
```

## Part A: Pivot Table

In this part, I used the training data to create a pivot table for CreditCard, Personal Loan and Online. This table helped me see how many customers accepted or did not accept the personal loan based on whether they have a credit card and use online banking.


```{r part-a}
table(train$CreditCard, train$Personal.Loan, train$Online)
```


From the table, I can see that 57 customers who have a credit card and use online banking accepted the personal loan, while 475 customers from the same group did not accept it.


## Part B: Probability Calculation

I calculated how likely a customer is to take a personal loan given that they use online banking and own a credit card. From my results in Part A, 57 customers accepted the loan and 475 rejected it within this group.


```{r part-b}
57 / (475 + 57)
```

The probability I got is 0.1071, which is around 10.71%. This means that out of 100 customers who have a credit card and use online banking, around 11 customers accepted the personal loan in the training data.


## Part C: Pivot Tables

For this part, I used the training data to make two pivot tables. The first table compares loan acceptance with online banking usage, and the second one checks loan acceptance against credit card ownership.


```{r part-c-online}
table(train$Personal.Loan, train$Online)
```

```{r part-c-creditcard}
table(train$Personal.Loan, train$CreditCard)
```

From the first table, I can see that 179 customers who use online banking accepted the personal loan. In the second table, 91 customers who have a credit card accepted the loan. These numbers will help me calculate the probabilities in the next part.


## Part D: Probability Calculations

```{r part-d}
# i. Credit card given loan accepted
91 / 278

# ii. Online banking given loan accepted
179 / 278

# iii. Loan accepted
278 / 3000

# iv. Credit card given loan not accepted
792 / 2722

# v. Online banking given loan not accepted
1620 / 2722

# vi. Loan not accepted
2722 / 3000
```

From these calculations, I found that 278 out of 3,000 customers accepted the personal loan, while 2,722 did not. I also calculated the probabilities for credit card ownership and online banking separately for both groups.



## Part E: Naive Bayes Probability

```{r part-e}
loan_yes <- (91 / 278) * (179 / 278) * (278 / 3000)
loan_no <- (792 / 2722) * (1620 / 2722) * (2722 / 3000)

loan_yes / (loan_yes + loan_no)
```


Using the Naive Bayes calculation, I got a probability of 0.1106, which is around 11.06%. This is the estimated chance of accepting a personal loan for a customer who owns a credit card and uses online banking.


## Part F: Comparison of Probabilities

The result from Part B was 10.71% since it directly calculated the exact ratio using the actual data, while Part E used the Naive Bayes formula to produce 11.06%. While Part B is entirely accurate for this training sample, it remains essential to analyze the validation data to determine which approach yields better predictions for new customers.


## Part G: Naive Bayes Model

```{r part-g-old}
library(e1071)

model <- naiveBayes(
  as.factor(Personal.Loan) ~
    as.factor(CreditCard) + as.factor(Online),
  data = train
)

model
```


```{r part-g-prediction}
new_customer <- data.frame(
  CreditCard = factor(1, levels = c(0, 1)),
  Online = factor(1, levels = c(0, 1))
)

predict(model, newdata = new_customer, type = "raw")
```

```{r part-g-model}
library(e1071)

train$CreditCard <- as.factor(train$CreditCard)
train$Online <- as.factor(train$Online)
train$Personal.Loan <- as.factor(train$Personal.Loan)

model <- naiveBayes(
  Personal.Loan ~ CreditCard + Online,
  data = train
)

model
```


### Part G: Conclusion

The probability of accepting a personal loan for a person with a credit card and online banking is 11.06% according to the Naive Bayes model. I also got the same result when I calculated it using the formula in Part E. The probabilities shown in the model matched the values I calculated in Part D.


## Final Conclusion

In this assignment, I worked with the UniversalBank dataset to see how having a credit card and using online banking are related to taking a personal loan. From the pivot table, I got 10.71%, and when I used Naive Bayes, I got 11.06%. The results were almost the same. By doing this assignment, I got a better idea of how to find probabilities from tables and how Naive Bayes works with the same data.
